title: House Votes 214-208 to Rebuke Trump's Iran War Powers
excerpt: Four Republicans crossed party lines to support a war powers resolution directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities in Iran, as the Senate prepares its own vote later Thursday.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • House passed a war powers resolution 214-208, rebuking Trump's Iran conflict management.
  • The resolution is symbolic and does not require presidential approval.
  • Defense Secretary requested $67 billion for the Iran campaign amid rising war costs.
  • Oil prices surged past $100 per barrel due to Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers.
  • The Senate is set to vote on a similar resolution later today.

Congress Challenges Presidential War Authority

The U.S. House of Representatives voted Thursday to halt military hostilities in Iran absent congressional approval, delivering the latest in a series of bipartisan rebukes to President Donald Trump's prosecution of the war.

https://x.com/dawn_com/status/2080309491476607250

The war powers resolution, led by Reps. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Jason Crow (D-Colo.), passed 214-208. Four Republican lawmakers — Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Tom Barrett of Michigan, and Warren Davidson of Ohio — crossed party lines to support the measure. These same four GOP members backed a similar resolution in June.

Jayapal and Crow forced the vote using a procedural tool known as a privileged resolution, which allows rank-and-file lawmakers to move legislation over the opposition of House GOP leadership.

"18 American servicemembers have been killed since this war began. Hundreds more have been injured. Billions of taxpayer dollars have been spent. The President's war with Iran has been an unmitigated disaster."

— Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colorado

Symbolic but Politically Potent

The concurrent resolution does not carry the force of law. Unlike joint resolutions, concurrent resolutions are not presented to the president for signature or veto, meaning the measure cannot compel the administration to withdraw forces even if the Senate passes its own version.

The Senate is expected to vote on a parallel measure later Thursday. In June, Republican senators briefly bucked the White House to pass a similar resolution before reversing course the following day. The upper chamber is currently operating with a narrower margin, with Sen. Mitch McConnell on medical leave.

Still, the vote forces every lawmaker to go on record less than four months before the November midterm elections, where the war's growing unpopularity could prove decisive in competitive districts.

War Costs Mount as Hegseth Seeks $67 Billion More

Thursday's vote landed just two days after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asked Congress for $67 billion in additional funding for the Iran campaign. The Pentagon has already spent $37.5 billion on the conflict, according to its own figures.

The request came as the House separately passed a $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act on Wednesday by a vote of 216-212, authorizing unprecedented military spending that includes funding for the Iran war, defense systems, and troop pay raises of up to 7 percent.

Democrats seized on the contrast between massive defense outlays and the administration's cuts to domestic social programs.

"What you just saw was the United States Congress doing its job, to take an up or down vote on matters of war and peace."

— Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colorado

Energy Markets Rattle as Conflict Widens

The congressional action coincided with a sharp escalation in the broader regional conflict. Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed responsibility Thursday for attacking two Saudi oil tankers attempting to exit the Red Sea — a critical alternative shipping route as U.S.-Iran hostilities have restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude surged more than 6 percent to $100 per barrel, its highest level since late May. West Texas Intermediate rose 5 percent to near $91 per barrel. The national average gasoline price stood at $4.09 per gallon Thursday morning, up from $3.93 last month and $3.16 a year ago, with analysts projecting prices could climb to $4.25-$4.40 in the coming weeks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking during a trip to Southeast Asia, said the Houthis had been "suckered into this by the Iranians" and urged de-escalation.

Diaspora Implications

The widening conflict carries direct consequences for Indian Americans and the broader Indian diaspora. Rising oil prices threaten India's energy security — the country imports more than 80 percent of its crude oil — and could fuel domestic inflation. Hundreds of thousands of Indian workers in Gulf states face heightened security risks as tensions spread across the region, particularly near the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea corridor.

Indian American families with members serving in the U.S. military also face mounting anxiety. Four American service members killed during the conflict were returned to the United States in flag-draped cases on Wednesday.

What Comes Next

The Senate vote later Thursday will test whether growing Republican dissent translates into a more durable challenge to the administration's war powers. Even if both chambers pass their resolutions, the measures remain non-binding. But the political signal is unmistakable: bipartisan patience with an open-ended military commitment in Iran is eroding, and lawmakers face increasing pressure from voters ahead of November to demonstrate accountability over the conflict's rising human and financial costs.
